questions.question: In the term 'spanning tree' of a connected undirected network, what does the word 'spanning' require of the selected tree?
options: That it contains every vertex of the network
That it contains every edge of the network
That it passes through every cycle of the network
That it gives every vertex exactly one edge

questions.question: An undirected network has two groups of vertices with no edge between the groups; inside each group every pair of vertices is joined by a path. Does the network have a spanning tree?
options: Yes, one tree per group together forms a spanning tree.
Yes, after adding an edge between the two groups.
No, since no tree on these edges reaches both groups.
No, since only a cycle-free network has a spanning tree.

questions.question: $T$ is a spanning tree of a connected undirected network with $n\ge2$ vertices. One edge of $T$ is deleted from $T$. What is true of the remaining selection of edges?
options: It still connects all vertices, since the network has other edges.
It no longer connects all vertices only if a leaf edge was deleted.
It now contains a cycle, since a tree with $n-2$ edges is unbalanced.
It no longer connects all vertices, whichever edge was deleted.

questions.question: An undirected network has vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ and edges $A$–$B$, $A$–$D$, $B$–$C$, $B$–$D$, $C$–$E$, $D$–$E$. Which edge set is a spanning tree of this network?
A spanning tree of a seven-vertex network consists of the edges 1–7, 1–4, 4–3, 3–6, 6–2 and 6–5. Which route inside this tree joins vertex 2 to vertex 7?
options: 2–6–5–7, using an edge from 5 to 7
2–6–5–6–3–4–1–7, a detour through 5
Several routes, one through each branch at 6
2–6–3–4–1–7, the only route in the tree

questions.question: A connected network has 10 vertices. A planner proposes a selection of 10 of its edges that reaches all 10 vertices as a spanning tree. What is wrong with the proposal?
options: It must contain a cycle, as a tree on 10 vertices has 9 edges.
Nothing, since 10 edges give each of the 10 vertices one edge.
It must leave a vertex unreached, since one edge is too many.
It must be disconnected, since 10 edges split into 2 groups.

questions.question: A spanning tree has the edges P–Q, Q–R, Q–S, S–T, S–U. The original network also has the edge R–T, which is added to the tree. Which cycle does this create?
options: No cycle, since R and T are both leaves of the tree
A cycle through all six vertices of the tree
R–Q–S–T–R, the tree path R–Q–S–T closed by R–T
Two cycles, one through Q and one through S

questions.question: Two analysts each find a spanning tree of the same connected undirected network with 9 vertices, and their trees are different. What must the two trees have in common?
options: Both trees contain exactly the same 8 edges.
Both contain all 9 vertices and exactly 8 edges.
Both trees have the same total edge length.
Both trees have at least one edge in common.

questions.question: For which connected undirected networks with $n$ vertices is there exactly one spanning tree?
options: Exactly for those networks that contain no cycle.
For none, since some edge can always be swapped.
Exactly for those where every degree is at most 2.
Exactly for those whose edge count equals $n$.

questions.question: Eight offices are to be linked by direct cables, chosen from a set of possible office pairs that connects all offices, so that every office can reach every other one. What is the smallest number of cables, and why?
options: 8, because each office needs its own cable to be connected.
28, because every pair of offices needs a direct cable.
4, because each cable links two of the eight offices.
7, because a smallest such selection is a spanning tree.

questions.question: A network has four vertices A, B, C, D with the edges A–B, B–C, C–D, D–A and the diagonal A–C. How many different spanning trees does it have?
A connected undirected network has 8 vertices and 8 edges, and it contains exactly one cycle, which has 5 edges. How many different spanning trees does the network have?
A selection of edges from a connected network with $n$ vertices contains all $n$ vertices and exactly $n-1$ edges. Is the selection necessarily a spanning tree?
options: Yes: $n-1$ edges on all $n$ vertices always form a tree.
No: a cycle in one part can leave another part cut off.
Yes, provided every vertex is an end of some chosen edge.
No: a spanning tree needs $n$ edges, one for each vertex.

questions.question: In a connected undirected network, $e$ is any edge joining two different vertices. Is there always a spanning tree that contains $e$?
options: Yes: add $e$ to any spanning tree, then drop another edge of the new cycle.
No: an edge lying on a cycle is always left out of every spanning tree.
Only if one endpoint of $e$ has degree 1, so that $e$ cannot be avoided.
Only if the network has no cycles, since then every edge is in the tree.

questions.question: A connected network has the cycle A–B–C–D–A, the edge D–E and the triangle E–F–G. Which edges belong to every spanning tree of this network?
options: D–E and the three edges of the triangle E–F–G
No edge, since every edge can be swapped out
Only D–E, since it is the one edge on no cycle
All edges at D or E, as they join the two parts

questions.question: A selection of edges in a network with 12 vertices contains all 12 vertices and no cycle, and it falls into 3 separate connected parts. How many edges does it have, and how many more edges are needed for a spanning tree?
options: 11 edges; no more edges are needed.
9 edges; 2 more edges are needed.
9 edges; 3 more edges are needed.
10 edges; 1 more edge is needed.

questions.question: Let $G$ be a connected undirected network. Which selection from $G$ is a spanning tree of $G$?
options: All vertices of $G$ with a subset of its edges that contains no cycle
Some of the vertices of $G$ with a subset of edges that is connected and has no cycle
All vertices of $G$ with any subset of its edges that keeps every vertex reachable
All vertices of $G$ with a subset of its edges that is connected and has no cycle

questions.question: $T$ is a spanning tree of a connected undirected network with $n$ vertices, and $e$ is an original edge joining vertices $u$ and $v$ that is not in $T$. Why does adding $e$ to $T$ always create a cycle?
options: Adding $e$ raises the degrees of $u$ and $v$, and a raised degree means a cycle.
It only does so if $u$ and $v$ are leaves, the vertices with a single edge in $T$.
Every edge of a connected network lies on a cycle, and $e$ brings that cycle into $T$.
$T$ already contains a path from $u$ to $v$, and $e$ closes it into a cycle.

questions.question: A spanning tree has the edges 1–2, 2–3, 3–4, 2–5, 5–6, 3–7. The original edge 4–6 is added. Which of the following tree edges can be removed so that the result is again a spanning tree, now containing 4–6?
options: The edge 1–2
The edge 3–7
The edge 2–5
No edge, since 4–6 keeps it a tree
